hn.originalTitle: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
hn.sourceOriginalText:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you | Michael Harley

In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some m.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone ???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp [1] , but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.

Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine ( https://versine.com ). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon. Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like: - Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app) - Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once - Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins) - Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this) Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0 We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer. Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as 1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP. Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval. Interestingl.

Comment 1: great job on building something that actually moves money using AI. to me this sounds like something CashApp and Venmo will copy pretty quickly.

Comment 2: Thank you! We see this as just a wedge into the complete agent-first banking solution we want to build, not a durable moat in itself. And on that front, we don't see this as something that an existing neobank can slap on to their existing solution: a lot of it has to be built from the ground up from first principles for agents. We're not just going to allow agents to do whatever humans can do with their bank, but actually even more - for example if I have a free trial renewal coming up, my agent can remind me to cancel, but it can't actually cancel on my behalf without logging in to the site. Why shouldn't it be able to tell my bank to decline a transaction from that merchant ahead of time? A lot of these decisions (like per-transaction authorization) aren't exposed to humans but should be to agents - which is what requires building this for agents first.

Comment 3: > And on that front, we don't see this as something that an existing neobank can slap on to their existing solution Could you explain why? Why couldn't I, if I ran a Neobank, create a Claude/ChatGPT plugin that can authenticate and use my existing API?

Comment 4: Cool idea! How do you make money?

hn.originalTitle: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models too unsafe to release
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Scoop: Anthropic and OpenAI employees fear unreleased AI models are too unsafe to release

Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem: Internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

Why it matters: The challenge could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the best AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen , sources told Axios.

Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models. Some insiders believe it's fixable. Others aren't convinced and say companies should stop training new models entirely.

Driving the news: Top AI leaders have long forecast that the technology would one day far surpass human intellect in virtually every field. Although internal models have yet to cross that threshold, recent breakthroughs at OpenAI and Anthropic have shocked researchers.

The rapid advances in reasoning across domains including math, science, cybersecurity and AI research have also made the models difficult, if not impossible, to contain or control in internal tests, the sources said.

Anthropic and OpenAI have unreleased models that are far more powerful than what they've already released publicly, but the AI companies have struggled to ensure that they are safe enough for public release, sources said.

This has led to debate within Anthropic, OpenAI and the AI research community about whether to stop releasing future frontier models publicly, instead reserving them for internal deployment only. There has also been debate around whether to train new models at all, sources inside and outside those companies told Axios.

What they're saying: "If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they're actually smarter than us ... they will in fact be able to trick us successfully," one researcher told Axios.

"And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we've had at work up until now sort of go out the window."

Catch up quick: The power of unreleased models is already on public display.

An Anthropic mathematician used an unreleased "research" version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which had eluded the brightest human minds for more than 150 years. An unreleased OpenAI model helped generate proofs for hundreds of math problems.

Unreleased AI models were responsible for some of the industry's most shocking safety events, including the Hugging Face hack.

Zoom in: AI researchers have long contemplated a terrifying threshold: If an AI possesses superhuman capability, how could humans contain it? Training practices that make AI models faster and more capable — but present greater safety risks — are widening the gap between what models can do and how well humans can control them.

Problem 1: Reinforcement learning. A primary AI model training method — where models learn through trial and error by receiving rewards for passing various tests — is one of the techniques driving rapid improvements in AI capabilities.

Why it's scary: As AI systems get more capable, they become better at "gaming" their rewards, including bypassing safety guardrails if cheating leads to a higher score.

Problem 2: They know they're being watched. Historically, researchers monitored AI safety by forcing models to "think out loud" — writing out step-by-step reasoning before outputting a final action or answer. This transparency was a safety net, allowing monitors to catch rule-breaking or dangerous logic in real time.

Why it's scary: As models grow more advanced, they are internalizing that logic, arriving at complex conclusions while showing less of their work. Researchers say the most advanced internal models have shown patterns of hiding reasoning entirely or providing deceptive "cover story" chains of thought to satisfy human monitors, sources say.

Threat level: In public statements, top AI leaders have spoken about these risks.

"This is the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," CEO Sam Altman wrote on X, citing his chief scientist's proposal for industry-wide limits on AI development.

"The speed of development is quickly becoming too fast for us to keep safe," Anthropic's alignment lead wrote on X in September, quoting an essay from CEO Dario Amodei about pacing the frontier, a sentiment he reiterated when the company went public.

Google Workspace Updates: Simplifying agent access while keeping organizations in control: MCP servers, CLI, standardized usage tiers, and admin policies

Simplifying agent access while keeping organizations in control: MCP servers, CLI, standardized usage tiers, and admin policies

As AI agents transform how people work, we want to make it simple for developers to build agentic workflows while keeping organizations in control of their data in Google Workspace. We are making Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and the official Workspace CLI generally available alongside standardized usage tiers to simplify how developers build and scale agents, paired with a new Workspace AI Tools Addendum and expanded enterprise controls over AI agents.

Simplifying and securing agent access with governed Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI

Developers now have two Google-managed ways to connect AI agents to Workspace without custom integration code:

Workspace MCP servers: Built on the open MCP standard, these Google-hosted servers let cloud and web-based AI agents securely connect to Workspace and call pre-built tools out of the box across Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks (with Keep coming soon). Explore supported MCP capabilities .

Workspace CLI: A command-line interface that brings Workspace tools directly to local environments, including developer terminals, VMs, and containerized sandboxes, for terminal-based agents. It includes packaged agent skills, dynamic command discovery, and scoped sign-in to read and update Workspace data. Explore the Workspace CLI .

Unlike traditional REST APIs, which are designed for deterministic app calls, both tools are purpose-built for dynamic agent workflows and provide:

Continuous improvements: Since Google fully manages these tools, agents that discover tools and schemas at runtime automatically benefit from ongoing improvements to context retrieval, credential setup, and tool accuracy.

Token efficiency: Rather than downloading raw data line by line via REST APIs, MCP tools return synthesized summaries within Workspace's boundary, and the CLI runs in the terminal, where agents can chain multiple tools. Both lower token costs and latency.

Streamlined security and compliance: Secure-by-default infrastructure with built-in user confirmations, audit logging, and admin controls helps streamline OAuth verification, Cloud Application Security Assessments, and enterprise security reviews without custom compliance work.

Standardizing the API usage tiers

In May, we announced a standardized usage model for Workspace APIs and MCP servers to give large-scale and AI tool developers a simpler, more predictable way to access higher quota while keeping Workspace infrastructure reliable for our entire community of developers.

Starting today , the Workspace APIs, including MCP servers and CLI, will have two usage tiers, starting with Gmail, Drive, and Calendar. Additional data access mechanisms will be updated similarly in the coming months.

Standard tier: No cost, with published usage quotas (rate limits).

Scaled tier: Designed for projects that need higher usage quota (rate limits).

Starting April 1, 2027 , if you select the Scaled tier, you will be charged only for API or MCP usage above any daily free allowances. If no action is taken, your projects may be throttled to the published usage quotas.

MCP requirement: AI agents or similar access tools must use MCP to access Workspace data, rather than calling Workspace REST APIs directly. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027 . Follow these steps to use MCP, and select the Scaled tier if you need higher quotas for agentic use.

Over 99% of active developers currently operate within the Standard tier and will continue to access these APIs at no additional cost. The same privacy, DLP, and data-protection standards apply across every tier.

If you are a Google Cloud Support customer, Workspace APIs will be excluded from the support variable fee calculation until at least December 2027 . Any changes will be communicated with at least 90 days' notice . To understand your options, see the Google Cloud Support packages .

Keeping organizations and users in control

Making it easier for developers to connect agents to Workspace goes hand in hand with giving organizations clear oversight and control of their data. We are extending the same governance principles customers rely on across Workspace to AI agents, so admins and users can get practical control over agents that access their data:

In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some m.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone ???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp [1] , but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

hn.originalTitle: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
hn.sourceOriginalText:
ClawDOS | An AI chat and coding harness for DOS, on a real IBM PC 5160 (8088 at 4.77 MHz)

An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card.

A (real) human’s note: Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. .

Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off.

The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS.

Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API.

From a sentence to a running program

One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running.

The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand.

WarGames, written on the XT

ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB.

Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor:

▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube

Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY , finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA.

It sees the screen

That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB:

And this is what Claude made of it:

Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do.

Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language.

A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy.

Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these:

A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/ . All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one.

Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories:

Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off.

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Maritime (YC F26) – A managed cloud for production AI agents
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime ( https://maritime.sh ). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. These were the primary points of friction: 1. Agent lifecycle management. There’s a lot that you have to build in order to properly give your agents VMs: things like sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery, and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. There are so many of these small sandbox management tasks that companies have to build and maintain themselves, and they add up. 2. Custom environments. Production agents have varying needs. Some agents need Windows applications. Others need Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software and applications, or specific dependencies. Some agents need access to private .

Comment 1: How do you compare yourself with https://www.agent37.com/ Also, digitalocean offers this now.

Comment 2: Better landing page animation, of course.

Comment 3: Agent37 is great if you want plain, cheap sandboxes. But you still have to build and manage a lot of the infra to sell agents to customers, we manage the entirety so that you don't think about cloud runtime at all and can focus on other things. We also provide you with ongoing support, an infra partner if you may. DigitalOcean is focusing on coding agent sessions in the cloud, rather than managing the things necessary to sell long living agents to customers.

Comment 4: There are a lot of alternatives in the market for this.

hn.originalTitle: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
hn.sourceOriginalText:
Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine ( https://versine.com ). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon. Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like: - Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app) - Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once - Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins) - Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this) Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0 We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer. Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as 1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP. Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval. Interestingl.

Comment 1: great job on building something that actually moves money using AI. to me this sounds like something CashApp and Venmo will copy pretty quickly.

Comment 2: Thank you! We see this as just a wedge into the complete agent-first banking solution we want to build, not a durable moat in itself. And on that front, we don't see this as something that an existing neobank can slap on to their existing solution: a lot of it has to be built from the ground up from first principles for agents. We're not just going to allow agents to do whatever humans can do with their bank, but actually even more - for example if I have a free trial renewal coming up, my agent can remind me to cancel, but it can't actually cancel on my behalf without logging in to the site. Why shouldn't it be able to tell my bank to decline a transaction from that merchant ahead of time? A lot of these decisions (like per-transaction authorization) aren't exposed to humans but should be to agents - which is what requires building this for agents first.

Comment 3: > And on that front, we don't see this as something that an existing neobank can slap on to their existing solution Could you explain why? Why couldn't I, if I ran a Neobank, create a Claude/ChatGPT plugin that can authenticate and use my existing API?

hn.summaryZh: 這篇來自 Hacker News 工程師討論，重點和 MCP 有關。適合用來快速了解社群正在討論的實作方向、工具變化或使用心得。
hn.sourceTextZh:
嘿 HN，我們是 Harshith、Param 和 Vishnu，我們正在建造 Versine ( https://versine.com )。 Versine 讓您只需與 AI 交談或發送簡訊即可發送和要求資金（想想帶有 MCP 的 Venmo）。我們是軟體工程師，曾在 Stripe、Databricks 和 Amazon 從事分散式系統工作。 Versine 是一款位於錢包前面並帶有餘額的 MCP。有了它，您的代理商可以執行以下操作： - 在您批准的情況下向某人匯款（透過我們應用程式中的金鑰） - 一次向最多 100 人發送資金或向其請求資金 - 向沒有 Versine 帳戶的人匯款（他們在 2 分鐘內向您可以將現金提現到銀行） - 未經您明確向受信任的聯絡人付款以下是一個示範：https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0 我們開始致力於此工作是因為助理令人沮喪的是，當涉及到金融和貨幣流動時，他們卻放手不管。你可以讓你的助手查看收據並列出所有欠款，並負責分攤小計、稅金、小費，但最後當你必須出去進行 Venmo 轉賬時，助手會將工作交還給你。我們目前的解決方案面向高級用戶：那些希望透過代理商實現一切自動化的用戶使用我們來分餐、團體旅行或結算撲克帳本。我們認為自己可以為一般消費者釋放更多價值： 1.

更多的人成為代理商的高級用戶，並且 2. 我們擴展到更完整的銀行解決方案：存款、轉帳、電匯，以及您可以透過 MCP 提供的銀行進行的所有操作（以及更多操作）。在幕後，每個用戶都有一個在 Base 上儲存 USDC 的自我託管穩定幣錢包。使用自我託管錢包，用戶擁有自己的金鑰，這意味著未經他們的批准，資金無法發送。有趣l。評論 1：在使用人工智慧建立真正可以轉移資金的東西方面做得非常出色。對我來說，這聽起來像是 CashApp 和 Venmo 很快就會複製的東西。評論2：謝謝！我們認為這只是我們想要建造的完整的代理優先銀行解決方案的一個楔子，而不是其本身的持久護城河。在這方面，我們不認為現有的新銀行可以將其強加到其現有解決方案：其中許多內容必須從代理商的首要原則開始建構。我們不僅允許代理人對銀行做任何人類可以做的事情，而且實際上甚至更多 - 例如，如果我即將進行免費試用續訂，我的代理人可以提醒我取消，但如果不登錄該網站，它實際上無法代表我取消。

為什麼它不能提前告訴我的銀行拒絕該商家的交易？許多這些決策（例如每次交易授權）不會暴露給人類，而應該暴露給代理——這就是需要首先為代理構建此決策的原因。評論 3：> 在這方面，我們不認為現有的新銀行可以將其應用到現有的解決方案上，您能解釋一下原因嗎？如果我運行 Neobank，為什麼我不能創建一個可以驗證和使用我現有 API 的 Claude/ChatGPT 插件？評論4：好主意！你怎麼賺錢？
